bib.title: CEDAR: Agent-Orchestrated Tree Search for Goal-Directed Optimization of Complex Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "CEDAR: Agent-Orchestrated Tree Search for Goal-Directed Optimization of Complex Systems", Yingtao Tian (Sakana AI, Tokyo), arXiv:2608.06871v1, 7 Aug 2026. The page footer says CC BY 4.0, and the text reads like a conference or ALife-venue submission. I treat it as a preprint.

COVERAGE: 125,503 chars extracted. I read chars 0 to about 104,000 closely: main text (pp. 1-8), references (skimmed), and the appendices through the start of the World Dynamics Judge/Editor transcripts. I skimmed the last ~17k chars (transcript text) and read the final ~1.5k. The extraction is clean. Nothing was garbled apart from flattened table check-marks (see PROBLEMS). The 35 pages are covered.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: CEDAR is MCTS in which an LLM Editor is the variation operator (patches the system's code) and an LLM Judge is the fitness function (a bounded score plus a text analysis). The tree is the population.
  number: none
  setup: Systems are a restricted Python subset (init, intermediates, derivatives, Euler step) with documented primitives. The Editor and Judge are Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5.1, run at default decoding settings.
  quote: "an LLM Judge evaluates emergent behavior against specified goals and an LLM Editor proposes improved variants, with the Judge acting as a fitness function and the Editor as a variation operator"
  where: p1 abstract
- claim: Against Optuna black-box search with 100 trials, CEDAR fitted a target trajectory with lower error. This held even though Optuna got the full ground-truth formulae and CEDAR got only a bare skeleton.
  number: CEDAR (GPT-5.1) L1 2.22, DTW 433.13. CEDAR (Claude) L1 3.29, DTW 757.21. Optuna with full formulae L1 3.71, DTW 477.52. Optuna with simple formulae L1 26.01, DTW 4927.94. Optuna with no formulae L1 29.06, DTW 5503.68.
  setup: A stochastic population model (3500 steps), one target run. DTW uses a Sakoe-Chiba band of w=250. Lower is better.
  quote: "CEDAR (Claude)✓3.29 757.21 / CEDAR (GPT-5.1)✓2.22 433.13"; "CEDAR, given no formulae, achieves lower error than the Optuna baseline given the full formulae."
  where: p7 Table 2
  caveat: The Claude run is worse than Optuna-full on DTW (757 vs 478). Only the GPT-5.1 run wins on both metrics. A second Optuna run scored L1 4.26, DTW 605.05 (Table 7, appendix).
- claim: The abstract-goal demo is a single run on Forrester's World Dynamics model. All three goals (population up, resource depletion down, pollution down) improved together. Optimizing one subgoal alone hurt the others. The two backends produced structurally different solutions.
  number: Judge text for the best node: "6.4x population growth with only 19.9% resource depletion". The baseline had 69% depletion and a 46x pollution increase.
  setup: 20 node selections with 5 expansions each (100 expansions). α=1, γ=2. The coefficient-only goal limits any change to 50%. The numbers come from the LLM Judge's own summaries, not an independent metric.
  quote: "Holy grail achievement - 6.4x population growth with only 19.9% resource depletion"
  where: p7 Table 3, appendix transcripts
- claim: Tree search beat linear search (an ablation). Tree context in the prompt was required. Without it "the expansion process fails to produce meaningful improvements".
  number: none (Fig. 8 gives only a qualitative comparison of node scores and trajectories)
  setup: Tested on the record-fitting task. Tree context was dropped in a "preliminary study", with no numbers given.
  quote: "our ablation against linear search (Figure 8) shows MCTS yields higher-scoring nodes and smoother trajectories that avoid overfitting-like behavior"
  where: p8; appendix "LLM Contextualization"
- claim: Tree search keeps solution diversity, so several near-best systems follow distinct trajectories. The authors say Optuna instead collapses to a single point.
  number: none
  setup: Nodes with scores close to the best, sampled from one run.
  quote: "All satisfy the goal, yet follow distinct trajectories: unlike the Optuna baselines, CEDAR avoids collapsing to a single overfitting-like point"
  where: p8 Fig. 7
- claim: Cost and runtime per search are modest.
  number: $10-$50 and about 30 minutes per run.
  setup: Depends on provider, expansion width and depth. The runtime is bound by LLM calls.
  quote: "Our runs incur moderate computational costs and runtime ($10–$50, 30 minutes per run)."
  where: p6
- claim: Node selection is a generalized UCT with progressive widening and a depth bonus. A node is expandable only while its expansion count is below τ.
  number: SCORE(v)=S_v + α·sqrt(ln(c_p+1)/(c_v+1)) + γ·DEPTH(v), with −∞ once c_v ≥ τ. α=1, γ=2.
  setup: The strategy is sampled uniformly from 8 prompts (breakthrough, aggressive, amplify, exploratory, targeted, contrarian, balanced, conservative).
  quote: "ϕ(·) = −∞ if c_v ≥ τ and α·√(ln(c_p+1)/(c_v+1)) + γ·DEPTH(v) otherwise"
  where: p4; Table 1
- claim: Robustness in the loop is handled with simple rules. Crashed or NaN runs get a low score, so the search backtracks on its own. LLM calls use structured outputs and up to three retries. An expansion that still breaks the constraints is discarded. The prompt also locks sections of the code (CONFIG, the Euler step, the OUTPUT section), marks "# NECESSARY" variables, and caps the Judge score at 10+2.5·depth.
  number: score <= 10.0 + 2.5 * depth
  quote: "assign crashed or NaN-valued runs a low score so MCTS naturally backtracks"; "IMPORTANT CONSTRAINT: Maximum possible score is score <= 10.0 + 2.5 * depth."
  where: p6; appendix "Scalability and Stability"; Judge prompt
- claim: The paper concedes that judge-editor circularity is an open risk.
  number: none
  quote: "The LLM Judge both scores candidates and shares a model class with the Editor, risking circularity, as the abstract-goal setting still relies on LLM judgment."
  where: p8 Conclusion

LIMITS
- Conceded by the authors: Judge and Editor share a model class (circularity). "We report trends rather than tight statistical claims, and the in-depth experiments focus on two systems." No systematic benchmark, and no comparison with classical evolutionary or multi-objective methods. The appendix says convergence and regret guarantees for MCTS with LLMs "remain open problems". The Judge reasoning is "not a verified causal account".
- Not shown: no held-out, matched-budget or multi-seed comparison beyond one Optuna rerun. The appendix says Optuna got 100 trials versus "10 MCTS iterations" for CEDAR. The main text says 20×5 = 100 expansions. These do not match, and I could not tell whether the 10 refers to a different setting. There is no ablation of Judge versus a programmatic metric in the abstract-goal task. Success there is judged by the Judge's own text plus three plotted variables. The Claude and GPT-5.1 runs found different trade-offs, with no repeats per backend. Only the Judge's text analysis supports the interpretability claim.
- Dated: it uses Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-5.1.
- Relevance to note 08: this is an LLM-Judge-plus-Editor search over simulation code. It is not an agent harness evolve loop. It fits only loosely as an example of "outer loop edits an artifact, a score gates it, and search keeps lower-scoring branches". The tree-versus-linear result and the diversity point echo the DGM archive argument that note 08 already makes.

BUILDS ON
- MCTS: Kocsis and Szepesvári (2006).
- Progressive widening: Chaslot et al. (2008), Inoue et al. (2025) (AB-MCTS "Wider or Deeper?", whose approach CEDAR adapts, since it came from Sakana).
- Depth bonuses: Blackshaw et al. (2025), Wu et al. (2025).
- LLM-as-variation-operator: Lehman et al. (2023) (Evolution through Large Models), Nisioti et al. (2024).
- ALife search: Kumar et al. (2025), Yamada et al. (2025).
- Compared against or contrasted with: Optuna (Akiba et al., 2019); LATS (Zhou et al., 2024); I-MCTS (Liang et al., 2025); GIF-MCTS (Dainese et al., 2024); DSPy (Khattab et al., 2024); Promptbreeder (Fernando et al., 2024).
- Domain: World Dynamics (Forrester, 1971), DYNAMO (Radzicki and Taylor, 2008), STELLA (Richmond, 1985), Hannon and Ruth (2014).
- Metric: DTW (Sakoe and Chiba, 1978).

CODE
- Appendix, minimal system in the restricted-Python representation (four parts: init, intermediates, derivatives, Euler step):
  `N = N + dt * dN` / `t += dt` inside `while t <= tf + 1e-12:`
- Editor guard text, worth quoting as a write-scope example: "Only change code between the "BEGIN ... / END ..." markers. DO NOT change imports, wrappers, loop structure, or OUTPUT section." Also "NEVER change simulation configuration parameters (dt, t0, tf, seed)".
- The Judge/Editor prompt templates (appendix) use `{goal} {code} {csv_data} {tree_context}`. The tree context shows diffs only against the current node.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1 (p3): CEDAR architecture. It shows select node and strategy, then Editor, run, Judge, update. This is the best single picture of the loop.
- Fig. 3 (p5): the expansion step with its prompts. It is useful to show that the tree context is part of the prompt.
- Fig. 5 (p7): the MCTS tree with the best path and scores, plus the before and after dynamics.
- Fig. 8 (p8): MCTS vs linear search. It is the only ablation evidence.
- Fig. 6 (p7): fitting comparison against Optuna.
- Fig. 4 (p6) and Fig. 10 (p25): single-objective optimization hurts the other goals. This supports the point that a single score hides trade-offs, which fits note 08's "structured, not scalar" argument.

PROBLEMS
- The Table 2 and Table 7 check-marks (Formulae No/S./F.) are flattened in the extraction. I assigned the Optuna rows to No, S. and F. from the text order and the prose ("no/simple-formulae variants are clearly worse"). The CEDAR rows are "no formulae".
- The appendix says CEDAR used "10 MCTS iterations" while the main text says 100 expansions (20 selections × 5). This is unresolved in the source.
- Appendix section numbers are blank ("Section ."), because appendix cross-references were stripped.
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF text.
- I did not read the full World Dynamics transcripts (about 17k chars). I read only their first and last parts.
